entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Dávid Baróti Szabó (1739–1819) stands as a foundational figure in the Hungarian Enlightenment and a pivotal architect of the modern Hungarian literary language. As a Jesuit priest, poet, writer, and linguist, his life's work was dedicated to elevating Hungarian to the status of a sophisticated literary medium capable of expressing complex classical and contemporary thought. Born in Baraolt, Transylvania, his extensive education within the Jesuit order provided him with a profound grasp of classical languages and rhetoric, which he later meticulously applied to the renewal of his native tongue, making him a central intellectual force during a period of burgeoning national consciousness in the Habsburg Monarchy.

His most enduring contributions include pioneering translations of classical Latin poets, notably Virgil's *Aeneid* (published in installments from 1782) and Horace's Odes, into refined Hungarian. These works were not mere literal renditions but artistic reinterpretations that demonstrated the expressive power and metric flexibility of Hungarian, setting new standards for poetic language. Alongside Ferenc Kazinczy and János Batsányi, Baróti Szabó co-founded and edited *Magyar Museum* (1787–1792), Hungary's first significant literary and scholarly journal, which became a vital platform for disseminating Enlightenment ideas and promoting linguistic reform. His grammatical treatises and lexicographical efforts further solidified the structure and vocabulary of Hungarian, directly influencing a generation of writers.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Dávid Baróti Szabó was a pivotal figure in the Hungarian Language Reform, whose classical translations and journalistic efforts fundamentally shaped the modern Hungarian literary language. His work set the stage for subsequent national literary development, making him a lasting influence on Hungarian culture.
